title: Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Jurisprudence of Incremental Innovation: A Comprehensive Analysis of Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner and the Transformation of the U.S. Research Credit
subject: Supply Costs / Qualified Research Expenses
summary: Union Carbide v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 2d Cir. 2012) is the leading U.S. federal case on claiming the Section 41 R&D tax credit for manufacturing plant process trials. It holds that raw materials a manufacturer would have purchased anyway for commercial production are not qualified research supplies, even when the process research itself qualifies.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The litigation in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, 97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207 (2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), cert. denied, 569 U.S. 904 (2013), stands as the preeminent United States federal tax precedent governing the eligibility of commercial plant trials and manufacturing process improvements for the Research and Experimentation (R&D) tax credit under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.). The dispute arose from aggressive affirmative tax credit claims asserted by Union Carbide Corporation and its consolidated subsidiaries (UCC), a premier global manufacturer of petrochemicals, olefins, and polyethylene plastics that subsequently became a wholly owned subsidiary of the Dow Chemical Company in 2001. The ruling establishes a rigorous statutory demarcation between routine commercial manufacturing costs and incremental research expenditures, while simultaneously defining the evidentiary threshold required to prove a scientific process of experimentation during full-scale production runs.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Procedural Posture

On its originally filed federal income tax returns for the 1994 and 1995 taxable years, UCC claimed approximately $18 million in research credits calculated under the traditional incremental methodology of I.R.C. § 41(a)(1). Those original return positions focused primarily on conventional laboratory and dedicated research-facility activities. Following the issuance of a statutory notice of deficiency by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, UCC filed a timely petition for redetermination with the United States Tax Court and raised affirmative claims seeking over $8 million in additional research credits for 1994 and 1995.

These additional claims centered on 106 separate manufacturing process improvement projects conducted directly on active commercial production equipment in various units within six of UCC's manufacturing plants; the representative projects tried to the court were conducted at UCC's Taft Plant and Star Plant, both located in Hahnville, Louisiana. In connection with these process trials, UCC sought to include as qualified research expenses (QREs) not only the wages of research engineers and plant operators, but also the entire cost of the raw hydrocarbon feedstocks and chemical monomers that passed through the commercial reactors during the experimental runs. Furthermore, because the consistency requirement of I.R.C. § 41(c) obliged UCC to determine its base period QREs on a basis consistent with its new credit-year claims, UCC recomputed its historical base period QREs for the 1984 through 1988 taxable years by adding plant-based research runs it had not originally included—an adjustment that increases, rather than reduces, its fixed-base percentage and base amount and therefore offsets part of the additional credit claimed for the 1994 and 1995 credit years.

To adjudicate the 106 disputed process projects efficiently, UCC and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agreed to try a representative sample comprising five of the largest claim projects. The first representative project was the Amoco Anticoking Project, conducted on furnace 24 in the Olefins-2 unit of the hydrocarbons unit at the Taft facility, which evaluated—under a secrecy agreement that gave UCC no license or patent rights—a pretreatment technology developed by Amoco that applied a dithiophosphoric acid derivative solution to the interior walls of the cracking coils to "poison" the tube-wall sites that promote catalytic coke formation during the thermal cracking of hydrocarbon feedstocks into ethylene. The second project was the UCAT-J Project, conducted on the two gas-phase fluidized-bed UNIPOL polyethylene reactors of the LP-3 unit at the Star facility, which tested the commercial-scale use and operating parameters of a high-activity Ziegler-Natta catalyst (UCAT-J) that is over four times more active than UCC's conventional M-1 catalyst. The third project was the Sodium Borohydride Project, conducted in the Olefins-2 acid gas removal system of the hydrocarbons unit, which tested the injection of a sodium borohydride solution into the caustic scrubber to remove acetaldehyde from the cracked furnace gas while the monoethanolamine (MEA) system was shut down for maintenance, so that UCC's crude butadiene would remain within its customer's 100 ppm acetaldehyde specification. The fourth project was the UOP GA-155 Project, conducted in the Olefins-1 fractionation section, which evaluated replacing UOP-5—a stabilizer previously injected into the dripolene product as it flowed out of the C4 column—with an alternative vendor formulation (UOP GA-155, which contained UOP-5's active ingredient plus a dispersant) injected into the C3 distillation column feed to suppress polymer fouling in the C3 column trays and reboilers. The fifth representative claim was the Spuds Project, also conducted in the hydrocarbons unit; after the claim-project trial, UCC moved for leave to amend its petition to withdraw the Spuds project and conceded that it did not satisfy the statutory criteria for qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d), but because the Tax Court denied that motion, the Court made an independent determination and held that the Spuds project failed the Section 174 Test.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Commissioner mounted a multi-tiered legal and factual challenge to UCC's refund claims. At the activity qualification level under I.R.C. § 41(d), the IRS argued that UCC's plant trials were routine production runs, vendor product validations, or minor operational adjustments that lacked objective technological uncertainty under I.R.C. § 174 and failed to employ a structured process of experimentation under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C). At the expenditure level under I.R.C. § 41(b), the IRS contended that even if a plant trial constituted qualified process research, the raw materials processed during the trial were ordinary commercial inventory that UCC would have purchased regardless of any research activity. Because those raw materials were converted into finished chemical and plastic goods sold to third-party customers in the ordinary course of business and deducted as Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), the IRS argued they were neither "used in the conduct of qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) nor direct research expenses under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1). Finally, the IRS argued that UCC had failed to substantiate its credit-year and base period activities and had relied on unreliable assumptions, estimates, and conclusory expert opinions, and contended that UCC's base amount recomputation failed the consistency requirement (codified at I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) during the years at issue and now at § 41(c)(6)) because UCC had not proven that it included all base period activities and costs similar to the claim projects.
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The court's analysis operated within the interlocking architecture of I.R.C. §§ 38, 41, 174, and 6001, alongside the corresponding Treasury Regulations. Under I.R.C. § 41(a)(1), a taxpayer may claim a general business credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of its current-year QREs over a statutory base amount. Because tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, the taxpayer bears the strict burden of proving entitlement under Tax Court Rule 142 and New Colonial Ice Co. v. Helvering, 292 U.S. 435, 440 (1934), the authorities on which the Tax Court relied, and statutory credit provisions are narrowly construed against the claimant.

To constitute "qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), an activity must satisfy four cumulative tests applied separately to each "business component" defined in I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B). First, under the Section 174 Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), costs must be incurred in the "experimental or laboratory sense," which requires that the activities be investigative in nature and intended to discover information that eliminates objective uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product or process. Second, under the Technological Information Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Third, under the Business Component Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), the taxpayer must intend to apply the discovered information to develop a new or improved business component, defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Crucially, I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) mandates the Plant Process Rule, which dictates that any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component must be treated as a separate business component distinct from the product being manufactured. This statutory separation interacts directly with I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), which categorically excludes research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component. If a business component as a whole fails the four-part test, the Shrinking-Back Rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) directs that the tests be reapplied to the most significant subset of elements until a qualifying subcomponent is isolated or the most basic element fails to satisfy the statutory requirements.

Fourth, under the Process of Experimentation Test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), "substantially all" (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under I.R.C. § 41(d)(3). The process of experimentation requires the systematic application of the scientific method: formulating a hypothesis, testing and analyzing data, and evaluating one or more alternatives capable of resolving the technical uncertainty.

Once an activity satisfies I.R.C. § 41(d), only specific expenditure categories qualify as in-house QREs under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A): wages paid to employees for "qualified services" (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)), and amounts paid or incurred for "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), supplies encompass any tangible property other than land, improvements to land, and depreciable property. However, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) explicitly excludes indirect research expenditures and general and administrative (G&A) expenses from in-house QREs.
The Court's Final Holding

Judge Goeke of the United States Tax Court issued a comprehensive 298-page memorandum opinion that split the project qualification determinations, ruled decisively in favor of the Commissioner on the supply expenditure issue, and largely accepted UCC's position on the base period issues. On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit (Judge Korman, a district judge sitting by designation, writing for a panel with Judges Straub and Pooler, with Judge Pooler joining fully but filing a separate concurrence) affirmed the Tax Court's denial of supply QREs for the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J projects and its holding that the Sodium Borohydride project was not qualified research.

Regarding project qualification under I.R.C. § 41(d), the Tax Court held—and it was undisputed on appeal—that only two of the five representative projects—the Amoco Anticoking Project and the UCAT-J Project—satisfied all four statutory tests as qualified process research. The Spuds Project was conceded by UCC and independently held by the Tax Court to fail the Section 174 test because UCC's own experience with one-hole spuds and the burner manufacturer's information eliminated any objective uncertainty, the UOP GA-155 Project was disqualified for failing the Section 174 test due to the absence of objective technological uncertainty, and the Sodium Borohydride Project was disqualified for failing the Process of Experimentation test because UCC failed to conduct post-testing data analysis or systematic hypothesis evaluation.

With respect to supply QREs for the qualifying Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J process projects, both the Tax Court and the Second Circuit disallowed UCC's claim for raw material feedstocks consumed during the commercial production runs. The courts held that raw materials purchased for routine commercial production and converted into salable finished inventory—costs that UCC would have incurred regardless of whether any process research occurred—are not supplies "used in the conduct of qualified research" under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). The courts reasoned that only additional supply costs incurred because qualified research was being performed could qualify; because Amoco supplied its pretreatment free of charge and UCC's claimed supply costs consisted solely of ordinary raw-material production costs, with no separately identified incremental supplies, the Tax Court allowed no additional supply QREs for either project.

Regarding wage QREs, the Tax Court disallowed the UCAT-J wage claim—an allocation of total Star plant wages based on the percentage of polyethylene produced during the UCAT-J runs—because UCC offered no evidence of which employees worked on the project or how much time they actually spent, and because UCC's own costing expert found that plant operator time did not vary significantly between experimental and normal production runs. Based on credible testimony, however, the Tax Court allowed wage QREs for the specific hours that two employees, Mr. Hyde and Mr. Tregre, spent on the Amoco Anticoking project ($835 for 1994 and $210 for 1995), while disallowing the hours claimed for a third employee who did not testify. Finally, the Tax Court accepted UCC's recomputation of its 1984–1988 base amount ($135,112,912 of additional base period QREs, increased by $283,654.80 for 1987 to correct a costing error), relying on Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to treat UCC's list of identified base period runs—including runs UCC later conceded—as a close approximation of all qualified base period research, and holding that UCC satisfied the consistency rule (then I.R.C. § 41(c)(4), now § 41(c)(6)(A)).
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A granular examination of the Tax Court and Second Circuit opinions reveals four foundational legal, technical, accounting, and evidentiary failures that dismantled the vast majority of UCC's claimed refund, together with a base period recomputation that, although largely accepted by the Tax Court, further reduced the credit by increasing the base amount. Understanding the mechanics of these failures is essential for structuring defensible R&D tax credit claims in industrial, chemical, and manufacturing environments.
The "Plant Process Trap" and the Disallowance of Commercial Production Supplies

The central legal battleground in Union Carbide stemmed from the structural tension between the Post-Commercial Production Exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and the Plant Process Rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C). Because UCC's finished chemical products (ethylene, propylene, and polyethylene resins) had long been in commercial production, UCC could not frame the products themselves as the qualifying business components without triggering automatic disqualification under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(A). To circumvent this statutory bar, UCC properly invoked I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), which treats a manufacturing process as a separate business component from the product being produced. By defining its business components solely as the production processes—specifically, the thermal cracking process in the Amoco Anticoking project and the catalytic polymerization process in the UCAT-J project—UCC successfully proved that its process improvements had not yet reached commercial production during the trials.

However, winning the business component argument under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) created a fatal secondary trap when UCC attempted to quantify its supply QREs under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). During the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J process trials, UCC had to run massive quantities of hydrocarbon cracking feedstocks and ethylene monomer gases through its full-scale commercial furnaces and reactors to observe how the pretreated furnace coils and the UCAT-J catalyst performed under real-world operating temperatures and pressures. UCC argued that under the plain, unambiguous text of I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)—which covers "any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research"—the raw material feedstocks were literally "used" during the trials because it was physically impossible to test an industrial chemical process in a commercial reactor without feeding raw materials into the unit. UCC further pointed out that Congress did not insert limiting adverbs such as "solely," "exclusively," or "primarily" before the word "used" in I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).

Both the Tax Court and the Second Circuit rejected UCC's literalist statutory construction, identifying three interconnected legal and accounting deficiencies in UCC's position. First, the Second Circuit applied a purpose-driven statutory interpretation to the phrase "in the conduct of qualified research," holding that UCC improperly fixated on the isolated verb "used" while ignoring its modifying prepositional phrase. Writing for the panel, the appellate court explained that the critical statutory language specifies the type of use toward which creditable supplies must be put. In UCC's plant trials, the raw hydrocarbon feedstocks were put toward the manufacture of commercial goods for sale, not toward the conduct of process research. When the business component is the process rather than the product, the raw materials are merely the objects upon which the production process acts to generate commercial revenue.

Second, the courts established a strict "would have incurred regardless" causation standard for process research supplies, ruling that costs of materials that a taxpayer would have incurred in routine commercial production regardless of whether any qualified research was being conducted cannot constitute QREs. Because UCC operated its Taft and Star plants continuously to fulfill customer orders, it would have purchased the exact same hydrocarbon feedstocks and monomer gases in the absence of the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J trials. Only additional supply costs incurred because qualified research was being performed could satisfy the statutory nexus; notably, Amoco supplied its pretreatment chemical free of charge, and UCC identified no incremental supplies for either project (its UCAT-J claim instead priced the catalyst precursor and other materials as ordinary production inputs), so no supply QREs were allowed.

Third, the Tax Court highlighted UCC's accounting treatment and invoked the anti-windfall principle, noting that UCC had originally booked the disputed raw materials as manufacturing inventory and deducted them as Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), eventually selling the resulting polyethylene and olefins to customers in the ordinary course of business. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), indirect research expenditures do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Finding that neither the statute nor Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) clearly resolved the boundary between direct and indirect supply costs, the Second Circuit invoked Chevron, U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984), and Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452 (1997), deferring to the Commissioner's interpretation, advanced in his brief, that supply costs are indirect research expenditures if they would have been incurred regardless of any research activities. As Judge Korman's opinion for the panel reasoned—after quoting an oral-argument colloquy in which UCC's counsel confirmed that UCC sought credit for all supplies used to make a product it would have produced and sold anyway—affording a credit for supply costs the taxpayer would have incurred regardless of any qualified research "simply creates an unintended windfall" inconsistent with the congressional purpose of incentivizing incremental R&D outlays.

From a broader jurisprudential perspective, this holding created a sharp doctrinal dichotomy in United States tax law between process business components and product or pilot model business components. In subsequent product-based cases such as TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009) (involving custom injection-molding tools sold to customers), Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd in part and vacated in part, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014) (involving custom-designed prototype vessels), and Stephens v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2022-118 (involving custom airflow systems), courts distinguished Union Carbide and allowed supply QREs for materials incorporated into products or pilot models where the product itself was the uncertain business component and the materials were purchased specifically to build and test that concept. Conversely, whenever the IRS can characterize a taxpayer's trial as improving a production process rather than a product or pilot model under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—as seen in recent agricultural and industrial litigation like J.G. Boswell Co. v. Commissioner—Union Carbide operates to strip out all baseline production supplies. Although taxpayers in current litigation increasingly argue that the Supreme Court's overruling of Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo undermines the Second Circuit's reliance on administrative deference in Union Carbide, the Tax Court's independent statutory reading of "in the conduct of qualified research" remains a formidable barrier against claiming routine production inventory as QREs.
Failure to Establish Objective Technological Uncertainty Under I.R.C. Section 174 (The UOP GA-155 Project)

The complete disqualification of the UOP GA-155 Project illustrates the lethal consequence of conflating operational vendor validation with investigative research under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and I.R.C. § 174. In the olefins fractionation train, hydrocarbon liquids in the C3 distillation column are susceptible to undesirable polymerization (fouling), which degrades heat transfer and clogs distillation trays. UCC had previously injected a stabilizer known as UOP-5 into the dripolene product as it flowed out of the C4 column, and initiated a project via Facility Operational Change Reviews (FOCRs 94-61 and 94-80) to replace it with a newer vendor formulation, UOP GA-155—which UOP represented would both stabilize the dripolene and mitigate fouling—injecting it into the C3 column feed.

UCC asserted that it faced technological uncertainty regarding whether UOP GA-155 would effectively inhibit polymer fouling in its specific C3 distillation column and what the optimal injection rate would be. The Tax Court rejected this contention and held that the UOP GA-155 project failed the threshold Section 174 Test.

The Court anchored its holding in the principle that whether technological uncertainty exists under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) is an objective test that depends on the information available to the taxpayer at the outset of the activity, citing Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582, 590–91 (1964). To be deductible under I.R.C. § 174, expenditures must be "investigative" in nature and expended in developing the concept of a model or process in the "experimental or laboratory sense". In the UOP GA-155 project, the chemical vendor (UOP), not UCC, had developed the inhibitor, performed the research to determine its effectiveness, reviewed UCC's process stream and operating conditions, and recommended the design UCC should use to inject it. The information available to UCC prior to the plant trial established that UOP GA-155 was capable of inhibiting fouling and provided the method for its injection. Consequently, UCC's plant run was not an investigative effort to discover unknown technological information or resolve design uncertainty; rather, UCC was merely confirming UOP's representations through its own testing, which the Tax Court held does not create uncertainty within the meaning of I.R.C. § 174 because a taxpayer may not turn its back on the available information in order to create uncertainty. Because the UOP GA-155 project failed the Section 174 gateway test, the Tax Court declined to evaluate the remaining three tests of I.R.C. § 41(d).
Failure to Execute a Structured Process of Experimentation and Post-Testing Analysis (The Sodium Borohydride Project)

Even where a taxpayer proves the existence of genuine technological uncertainty under I.R.C. § 174, the activity will fail if the taxpayer does not resolve that uncertainty through a rigorous scientific method. This failure doomed the Sodium Borohydride Project, in which UCC injected sodium borohydride into the caustic scrubber of the Olefins-2 acid gas removal system to remove acetaldehyde from cracked furnace gas while the MEA system was shut down, so that its crude butadiene would remain within its customer's 100 ppm acetaldehyde specification.

Unlike the UOP GA-155 project, the Tax Court acknowledged that the Sodium Borohydride research activities were designed to resolve uncertainty: although the capability of sodium borohydride to remove acetaldehyde was generally known, UCC was uncertain whether it was the appropriate method given its high cost and unknown efficiency when reacting with a gas stream in a full-scale caustic scrubber, and whether UCC's design for injecting it was appropriate. Nevertheless, the Tax Court held—and the Second Circuit affirmed—that the project failed the Process of Experimentation Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C).

Synthesizing the statutory text with Black's Law Dictionary and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the Tax Court defined the requisite "process of experimentation" as requiring the application of the scientific method: an analytical technique by which a hypothesis is formulated and then systematically tested through observation, experimentation, and thorough data evaluation. While a process of experimentation need only evaluate a single alternative if only one is tried, the process generally must be capable of evaluating more than one viable alternative, and—most critically—the taxpayer must analyze the experimental results to refine or retest the hypothesis.

UCC's evidentiary failure in the Sodium Borohydride project occurred in the post-injection phase. After injecting the sodium borohydride into the process stream, UCC failed to perform systematic post-testing analysis or comparative evaluation of the operating data collected during the run. Specifically, the Tax Court noted that the data collected during the run were never documented in a final project report, that UCC instead treated a January 9, 1995 R&D report—prepared before the test occurred—as the functional equivalent of a project report, and that there was no evidence UCC experimented with or determined optimal dosages or injection rates. As the Tax Court emphasized, data collection alone, no matter how extensive, does not constitute a process of experimentation if it is not followed by meaningful analysis, and the Second Circuit affirmed this holding for the reasons stated in the Tax Court's review of the record. Simply introducing a chemical variable into a plant unit and observing operations without systematic data logging, post-test analytical comparison, and iterative hypothesis testing falls short of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C)—a standard subsequently invoked by the Tax Court to disallow undocumented milling trials in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and by the Seventh Circuit in rejecting ship construction claims in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023).
Over-Inclusion of Routine Plant Operator Wages and Deficiencies in Expert Wage Substantiation

With respect to employee compensation under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), UCC committed two distinct errors: claiming wages without distinguishing qualified research services from ordinary production labor, and failing to substantiate the time its plant personnel actually devoted to qualified research.

First, for the qualifying Amoco Anticoking project UCC claimed only the wages of three named employees (Mr. Hyde, Mr. Tregre, and Mr. Gorenflo) for a total of 52 estimated hours, whereas for the UCAT-J project UCC claimed a share of the total wages paid to all Star plant personnel—who supported the reactors 24 hours a day on rotating shifts—allocated by the percentage of Star's polyethylene production made during the UCAT-J runs (2.1 percent in 1994 and 4.18 percent in 1995). UCC argued that the projects could not have occurred without the employees who were operating the plant, so that their wages, like the raw materials, were QREs.

The Tax Court rejected this broad sweep, applying the exact same causal logic to production wages that it applied to production supplies. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" encompasses services immediately supporting individuals engaging in or directly supervising qualified research (such as a laboratory machinist fabricating an experimental rig or a technician logging research-specific sensor data), but excludes general and administrative services and other services that only indirectly benefit research activities. Because UCC's own costing expert found that the time spent by Star's plant operators and other support staff did not vary significantly between experimental UCAT-J runs and normal production runs, the Court concluded that those employees were engaged in ordinary production activities, and UCC offered no way of distinguishing wages paid for qualified research from wages paid for production. The Tax Court held that only wages attributable to services that would not normally have been provided could qualify, allowing $835 for 1994 and $210 for 1995 for the hours Mr. Hyde and Mr. Tregre credibly testified they spent planning the tests, participating in the pretreatments, and sending data to the technical center for analysis, while disallowing Mr. Gorenflo's two claimed hours because he did not testify.

Second, UCC lacked a contemporaneous project-based time-tracking system that recorded the exact hours engineers, scientists, and technicians devoted to each of the 106 process projects. To reconstruct its credit-year wage QREs for litigation, UCC's costing expert, Ms. Wendi Hinojosa, multiplied wage rates derived from employees' Forms W-2 by the hours the employees estimated they had worked on the Taft projects and, for the UCAT-J project, allocated Star budget-report wages by production volume, because UCC's preferred wage records (account levels) were unavailable for the credit years; separately, for the base period, Dr. Parvez Wadia's MATRIC team identified plant-based runs and estimated their durations and production quantities, and Ms. Sheri Toivonen of Ernst & Young costed them using UCC's product cost detail reports (PCDs) and material accounting summary reports (MASs).

The Tax Court noted flaws in parts of UCC's methodology; specifically, Ms. Toivonen did not independently verify the MATRIC team's run durations and production quantities, and Dr. Wadia kept no record of the projects he rejected, but the Court held that these flaws were cured by UCC's concession of additional runs (runs 807 through 820) and that Ms. Toivonen's reliance on Dr. Wadia was justified. However, unlike subsequent cases where taxpayers offered zero objective evidence to anchor an estimate—such as Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, aff'd, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014)—UCC introduced substantial contemporaneous technical documentation, including run plans, run notebooks, FOCRs, project reports, and cost accounting records, coupled with credible testimony from employees who executed the projects. Consequently, the Tax Court invoked Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540, 543–44 (2d Cir. 1930), in the base period context, accepting UCC's list of identified runs (including its concessions) as a close approximation of all qualified base period research while noting that UCC "must bear the consequences of its own inexactitude"; for the credit-year wages, by contrast, the Court allowed only the specific hours supported by testimony rather than estimating any additional amounts.
Base Period Recomputation and the I.R.C. Section 41(c) Consistency Rule

The final pillar of UCC's litigation strategy involved an adjustment of its historical base period computations (covering 1984 through 1988) under I.R.C. § 41(c). Under the regular credit regime, the "base amount" is the product of the taxpayer's "fixed-base percentage" (the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for tax years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989) and the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts for the four taxable years preceding the credit year.

When UCC filed its affirmative claims adding 106 commercial plant process projects to its 1994 and 1995 credit years, it implicated the Consistency Rule now codified at I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A) (codified as I.R.C. § 41(c)(4) during the years at issue) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d). The Consistency Rule mandates that the QREs taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year. As the Tax Court articulated in Union Carbide, the taxpayer must include the exact same types of research activities and the same categories of costs as QREs in both the credit years and the 1984–1988 base period.

UCC's base amount recomputation was challenged on two distinct fronts, and the Tax Court largely rejected both challenges. First, because UCC sought to include plant-level process improvement activities and production supply costs in 1994 and 1995 that it had omitted from its original 1984–1988 base period figures, it was required to identify and capture all analogous plant-level projects conducted between 1984 and 1988; the Court found—relying on Dr. Wadia's identification of 793 runs, UCC's concession of runs 807 through 820, and the testimony of 17 fact witnesses—that UCC had satisfied this duty, that the consistency rule applies at the level of the legal entity (UCC) rather than the entire controlled group, and that 138 polypropylene runs conducted for Seadrift Polypropylene Co. were properly excluded. Second, the Court held that Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) requires no particular type of document (such as the base period FOCRs UCC had destroyed), found UCC's records sufficient to substantiate the identified runs, and found Ms. Toivonen's costing methodology generally consistent with the credit-year methodology, treating her inclusion of ordinary production costs as harmless because it overstated the base amount and thereby reduced the credit. The Tax Court therefore accepted UCC's base period computation of $135,112,912 in additional base period QREs, increased by $283,654.80 for 1987 to correct the costing of the acrolein refining system capacity test.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement adjudicated in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner against the specific legal or evidentiary failures exhibited by the taxpayer and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court and the Second Circuit.

headers: Taxpayer's Legal, Technical, or Evidentiary Failure
Court's Governing Standard of Proof & Holding

cells: Section 174 Test: Objective Technological Uncertainty (I.R.C. §§ 41(d)(1)(A), 174(a); Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1))
UOP GA-155 Project (Replacing the UOP-5 dripolene stabilizer with UOP GA-155 injected into the C3 column feed to reduce fouling)

Taxpayer claimed uncertainty regarding how a vendor-supplied chemical inhibitor would perform in its distillation column, despite existing vendor data establishing the chemical's properties and anti-fouling capability.

Objective Information Standard: Uncertainty is measured objectively based on information available to the taxpayer at the outset. Activities must be "investigative" in the laboratory or experimental sense; confirming a vendor's representations through the taxpayer's own testing does not create uncertainty. Held: Disqualified.
Technological Information & Business Component Tests (I.R.C. §§ 41(d)(1)(B), 41(d)(2)(B)–(C), 41(d)(4)(A))
Amoco Anticoking & UCAT-J Projects (Furnace coil pretreatment & high-activity polyethylene catalyst trials)

Taxpayer's finished olefin and polyethylene products were already in commercial production under § 41(d)(4)(A). Taxpayer also initially included the Spuds Project, which lacked objective technological uncertainty.

Separate Plant Process Rule: Under § 41(d)(2)(C), a commercial production process is a separate business component from the manufactured product, avoiding the post-commercial production exclusion for the process itself. Held: Amoco & UCAT-J Qualified; Spuds Conceded and Independently Held to Fail § 174.
Process of Experimentation Test (I.R.C. §§ 41(d)(1)(C), 41(d)(3); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6))
Sodium Borohydride Project (Injecting chemical into the caustic scrubber to remove acetaldehyde while the MEA system was down)

Taxpayer injected the chemical into the unit but failed to perform systematic post-testing analysis or compare empirical run data against a hypothesis (e.g., no final project report documented the run data, and UCC relied on a January 9, 1995 R&D report prepared before the test).

Scientific Method Standard: Substantially all (80 percent or more) of activities must follow the scientific method—formulating a hypothesis, systematically testing viable alternatives, and performing post-test data analysis and comparison, rather than simple validation testing. Held: Disqualified (affirmed by the Second Circuit).
Shrinking-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2))
Disqualified Process Projects (UOP GA-155 & Sodium Borohydride)
The UOP GA-155 and Sodium Borohydride projects failed at the threshold § 174 and process-of-experimentation tests, respectively; the opinion identifies no qualifying subset of either project.

Iterative Subset Standard: If an overall business component fails § 41(d), the four-part test is reapplied to the most significant subset of elements; the rule is not itself a reason to exclude activities, and the Tax Court applied it to isolate the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J research activities from ordinary production activities. Held: Applied to sustain the Amoco & UCAT-J research activities; not applied to rescue UOP GA-155 or Sodium Borohydride.
Supply QREs: "Used in the Conduct of Qualified Research" (I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), (C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1))
Raw Material Feedstocks in Amoco Anticoking & UCAT-J Projects (Hydrocarbon gases & ethylene monomers)

Taxpayer claimed the full raw-material production costs of the trial runs, processed into salable finished goods, without separately identifying any incremental supplies, arguing the process could not be tested without running raw materials through the plant.

Incremental / "Would Have Incurred Regardless" Standard: Raw materials used to produce commercial goods for sale (accounted for as inventory/COGS) that would have been purchased regardless of the research are non-qualifying production/indirect costs. Only additional supplies used specifically to perform the research qualify. Held: Raw Materials Disallowed; No Additional Supply QREs Established.
Wage QREs: "Direct Support" vs. Routine Production Labor (I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), (B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)–(d))
Plant Personnel Wages at Taft & Star Facilities (Amoco Anticoking & UCAT-J runs)

For UCAT-J, taxpayer allocated a production-based share of all Star plant wages without identifying which employees worked on the project or their hours; for Amoco, it claimed estimated hours for three employees, one of whom did not testify.

Qualified Services Standard: Wages for services that would have been provided regardless of the research are not qualified services; only substantiated wages for services that would not normally have been provided qualify. Held: UCAT-J Wages Disallowed; Amoco Wages Allowed Only for Mr. Hyde & Mr. Tregre ($835 for 1994 / $210 for 1995).
Recordkeeping & Judicial Estimation of Wage QREs (I.R.C. § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); Cohan Rule)
Engineering & Scientific Wage Allocations (Claim Projects & Base Period Identified Runs)

Taxpayer lacked contemporaneous project timesheets; credit-year wages rested on employee hour estimates and a production-based allocation, and base-period figures relied on expert determinations in which Ms. Toivonen did not independently verify the MATRIC team's (Dr. Wadia's) run durations and production quantities, and Dr. Wadia kept no record of rejected projects.

Cohan Approximation Standard (Base Period): Where records are imperfect but a reasonable basis exists, the court may accept a close approximation, and the taxpayer bears the consequences of its own inexactitude; specific credit-year wage hours require credible substantiation. Held: Credit-Year Wages Allowed Only Where Supported by Testimony; Base-Period Run List Accepted Under Cohan After Concessions.
Base Amount & Consistency Requirement (I.R.C. § 41(c)(1), (c)(6)(A) (formerly (c)(4)); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-3(d))
1984–1988 Base Period QRE Recomputation (Fixed-Base Percentage calculation)

Taxpayer added plant process claims in the credit years, requiring a consistent recomputation of base period QREs; the Commissioner argued UCC's identification of base period activities was incomplete (e.g., base period FOCRs had been destroyed) and its costing inconsistent.

Methodological Parity Standard: Taxpayer must include the same types of activities and cost categories in both the credit year and the base period; no particular type of document is required so long as records substantiate the claim. Held: Base Recomputation Accepted ($135,112,912, plus $283,654.80 for 1987).

body.text: Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner into actionable legal and tax engineering protocols, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial projects confronting the exact statutory pitfalls that defeated UCC's claims. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract and accounting terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the court's objections and satisfy I.R.C. § 41.
Case Study 1: Continuous Petrochemical Cracking and Distillation Process Optimization
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

Olefins Dynamics Corp. (ODC) is a United States petrochemical manufacturer operating a continuous steam-cracking and light-olefins fractionation complex on the Gulf Coast. During the current taxable year, ODC undertakes Project Alpha-7, a dual-phase plant initiative aimed at introducing a novel organometallic coil-passivation additive from a third-party specialty chemical supplier into its naphtha cracking furnaces to suppress pyrolytic coke formation, while simultaneously injecting a newly formulated anti-fouling dispersant into its downstream depropanizer distillation column to reduce reboiler polymerization.

During the 45-day full-scale plant trial, ODC processes $42 million of naphtha feedstock through the furnaces and depropanizer, converting the hydrocarbon stream into commercial-grade ethylene and propylene that ODC sells to existing customers under long-term off-take contracts. ODC's tax department intends to claim the entire $42 million of naphtha feedstock as supply QREs under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), 100 percent of the wages of the 36 shift operators staffing the olefins unit during the 45-day trial under I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), and the engineering wages associated with both the furnace passivation trial and the depropanizer dispersant run. Currently, ODC has only a two-page Management of Change (MOC) authorization form and vendor product brochures on file, and its engineers plan to rely on year-end memory estimates for time allocations.

Without immediate remedial restructuring, ODC's claim will collapse under audit and Tax Court scrutiny in a manner directly parallel to Union Carbide. The depropanizer dispersant phase mirrors the UOP GA-155 Project and will fail the Section 174 Test because relying on vendor brochures without proving objective chemical or thermodynamic uncertainty in ODC's specific column configuration reduces the run to routine vendor validation. Furthermore, if ODC fails to log and mathematically analyze post-trial fouling and pressure-drop curves against pre-trial baselines, both phases will fail the Process of Experimentation Test under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), mirroring the Sodium Borohydride Project. Finally, the $42 million naphtha feedstock claim and the 36 shift operators' baseline wages will be disallowed in full under the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J holdings because the naphtha is routine inventory sold to customers that ODC would have purchased regardless of the trial, and the shift operators are performing routine commercial production.
Step 1: Project Governance and Business Component Bifurcation

ODC must immediately restructure its internal project governance before initiating the plant trial by replacing the generic MOC form with a formal Research & Experimental Protocol Charter (REPC) that bifurcates Project Alpha-7 into two distinct process business components under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C). Business Component 1A must be explicitly defined as the Pyrolytic Cracking Coil Passivation Process—specifically, the high-temperature metallurgical passivation process inside the radiant furnace tubes, wholly separate from the commercial ethylene product. Business Component 1B must be defined as the Depropanizer Kinetic Fouling Inhibition Process.

To avoid the UOP GA-155 Section 174 trap on Business Component 1B, ODC must not frame the trial as testing an off-the-shelf vendor chemical. Instead, ODC's process engineering team must conduct a pre-trial Objective Uncertainty Audit documenting why publicly available literature and the vendor's technical data sheets cannot predict the reaction kinetics in ODC's depropanizer. Specifically, the charter must establish that ODC's cracked-gas feedstock contains elevated diolefin and acetylenic contaminants at pressures and residence times outside the vendor's known operating envelope, creating objective engineering uncertainty regarding whether the dispersant will induce secondary phase-separation or catalyst poisoning in downstream hydrogenation reactors. If no such objective design or method uncertainty exists, ODC's tax governance committee must voluntarily exclude Business Component 1B from its R&D claim at the outset rather than tainting the credibility of its entire filing.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Scientific Method Execution

To overcome the Sodium Borohydride failure under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1)(C), ODC must mandate a structured scientific documentation workflow within its Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) and Distributed Control System (DCS) historian. Prior to chemical injection, engineers must record formal, falsifiable quantitative hypotheses in the REPC—for example, hypothesizing that continuous injection of 150 ppm organometallic passivator during steam-air decoking will form a uniform chromium-alumina barrier layer that reduces the catalytic coking rate constant (k<sub>c</sub>) by at least 35 percent over a 30-day run length without increasing radiant coil tube-skin temperatures above the coils' metallurgical design limit.

Rather than executing a single validation pass, ODC must structure the trial to evaluate multiple viable alternatives across parallel furnace cells, running Furnace 1 as an untreated baseline control, Furnace 2 with pre-passivation soaking only, and Furnace 3 with continuous passivator dosing at varying parts-per-million thresholds. Crucially, unlike UCC's Sodium Borohydride project—for which the run data were never documented in a final project report and UCC relied instead on an R&D report dated January 9, 1995, prepared before the test—ODC must require a mandatory Post-Trial Engineering Evaluation Report containing time-series DCS plots of coil transfer-line exchanger (TLE) pressure drops, gas-chromatograph effluent compositions, and metallurgical coupon analyses. This closing report must statistically compare the empirical data from Furnaces 1, 2, and 3 against the initial hypothesis, documenting failure modes and iterative parameter adjustments to prove a complete process of experimentation.
Step 3: Accounting Segregation of Incremental Supplies Versus Commercial Feedstocks

In strict compliance with the Second Circuit's holding in Union Carbide, ODC must configure its ERP cost-accounting system to prevent the commingling of commercial inventory costs with direct research supplies. ODC must exclude 100 percent of the $42 million of naphtha feedstock from its QRE calculation, leaving those costs in raw material inventory and COGS. Simultaneously, ODC must establish a dedicated Internal R&D Order and Sub-Ledger Account under I.R.C. § 174 to capture exclusively the additional tangible supplies purchased and consumed to conduct the experiment.

This segregated R&D supply account will properly capture the cost of the organometallic passivation chemicals and experimental dispersant batches, temporary injection quills, non-depreciable sacrificial metallurgical test coupons, and specialized sampling cylinders installed solely for the 45-day trial. It will also capture laboratory reagents and carrier gases used in additional gas-chromatography tests required by the REPC, as well as any off-specification hydrocarbon batches that are destroyed or flared—and never sold to customers—solely as a result of pushing Furnace 3 to an extreme experimental failure boundary during a test protocol.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Labor Tracking and Base-Period Consistency Verification

To eliminate reliance on vulnerable Cohan estimates and survive IRS scrutiny of plant operator wages and base-period consistency, ODC must exclude the baseline shift wages of the 36 plant operators. In their place, ODC must deploy a Research Task Exception Log integrated into the control room electronic shift book. Whenever an operator steps outside routine production duties to perform a research-specific action—such as calibrating the temporary chemical injection skid, pulling manual furnace effluent samples every four hours per the REPC, or executing experimental decoking temperature ramps—the operator must log the exact start and stop timestamps against Project Code Alpha-7. For process engineers and R&D chemists, ODC must require weekly electronic timesheet certification cross-referenced against their annual performance goals, thereby avoiding the evidentiary gap identified by the Tax Court in Union Carbide, where UCC offered no evidence of which employees worked on the UCAT-J project or how much time they actually spent on it. Finally, under I.R.C. § 41(c)(6)(A) (or the three-year rolling average if electing the Alternative Simplified Credit under I.R.C. § 41(c)(4)), ODC must audit its historical base-period records to ensure that its base-period QREs include all analogous incremental process trial supplies and engineering hours from the comparison years, maintaining strict methodological symmetry.
Case Study 2: Custom Biopolymer Pilot-Scale Development Versus Commercial Manufacturing
Scenario and Pitfall Alignment

BioResin Innovations Inc. (BRI) is a specialty chemical and advanced materials manufacturer that produces high-performance biodegradable polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) resins. BRI enters into a development and supply initiative (Project Zeta) to develop a new ultra-high-molecular-weight PHA resin grade engineered for subsea cable insulation. Rather than building a small laboratory bench reactor, BRI decides to develop and test the new resin formulation and fermentation-polymerization synthesis directly inside Line 4, one of its mid-sized commercial polymerization lines, using a custom-synthesized metallocene catalyst system.

Over a six-month campaign, BRI conducts 18 full-scale production batches on Line 4, consuming $6.5 million in bio-monomer raw materials, sugars, and solvents. Twelve of the batches fail to achieve the required dielectric and tensile strength specifications for subsea cables, but still meet the lower specifications for BRI's standard agricultural film resin; BRI re-labels those 12 batches and sells them to agricultural film distributors at standard market prices. The remaining 6 batches achieve the target subsea cable specifications and are sold to a marine cable manufacturer under a commercial purchase order. On its tax return, BRI characterizes Project Zeta as a "process improvement project" for Line 4, claims the entire $6.5 million of bio-monomers and solvents across all 18 batches as supply QREs, and relies on an outside R&D tax credit consulting firm to interview the Vice President of Manufacturing two years after the tax year to estimate that 75 percent of all plant personnel time was spent on Project Zeta.

Under the legal framework of Union Carbide and subsequent case law, BRI faces catastrophic disallowance. By characterizing the business component as the Line 4 manufacturing process while selling all 18 batches (12 as agricultural film and 6 as marine cable resin) in the ordinary course of business, BRI falls squarely into the Union Carbide holding, resulting in the complete disallowance of the $6.5 million of bio-monomers and solvents as commercial production inventory and COGS. Even if BRI attempts to pivot during audit and argue that the batches were products or pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—invoking TG Missouri, Trinity Industries, and Stephens—the IRS will argue, just as it did in J.G. Boswell and Union Carbide, that selling 12 batches into the standard agricultural commodity market proves those runs were standard commercial production whose supply costs would have been incurred regardless. Moreover, relying on a single unverified executive interview two years post-hoc without underlying technician verification will be rejected under the substantiation principles applied in Union Carbide—where the Tax Court disallowed the UCAT-J wage claim because UCC offered no evidence of how much time Star employees actually spent on the project, and disallowed claimed hours for an employee who did not testify—and the strict substantiation rules of Shami.
Step 1: Business Component Restructuring—Product and Pilot Model Designation

To escape the Union Carbide process-supply disallowance rule, BRI must fundamentally restructure how Project Zeta is defined, governed, and physically executed prior to commencing the trials. Instead of designating the Line 4 manufacturing process as the business component, BRI's R&D governance charter must designate the Subsea Dielectric PHA Resin Formula (Product Code PHA-900X) as a new product business component under I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B), and specifically classify the experimental batches produced during development as pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a "pilot model" is defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. As the Tax Court recognized in Stephens v. Commissioner when distinguishing Union Carbide, when supplies are purchased specifically to build a prototype or pilot model product to test technical concepts—and not for routine commercial inventory—Union Carbide does not foreclose treating those material costs as supply QREs.

To defeat an IRS argument that the runs are disguised commercial production, BRI must physically, operationally, and conceptually isolate the PHA-900X development trials from its commercial agricultural film runs. Whenever Line 4 is taken offline from commercial operations to run a PHA-900X experimental batch, BRI must issue a formal R&D Line Quarantine Directive that halts standard production scheduling, scales down batch sizes to the minimum volume physically required to achieve fluid-dynamic similarity in the reactor, and routes the output to a quarantined R&D testing warehouse rather than commercial finished-goods inventory.
Step 2: Contractual and Inventory Accounting Restructuring to Eliminate the "Routine Inventory" Taint

Because the single most damaging fact in Union Carbide was that the taxpayer processed raw materials booked as ordinary inventory/COGS and sold the resulting output into its standard commercial market, BRI must overhaul its commercial contracts and inventory accounting. First, BRI must prohibit the diversion of failed experimental batches into commodity inventory, ceasing the practice of re-labeling off-specification experimental PHA-900X runs and selling them as standard agricultural film resin. Selling failed experimental batches into an existing commodity market allows the IRS to argue that the bio-monomer supplies would have been purchased anyway to satisfy BRI's agricultural film sales volume. Instead, failed experimental batches must be retained for destructive dielectric testing, recycled into dedicated experimental rework loops, or scrapped with documented waste-manifest certificates.

Second, for the pilot batches delivered to the marine cable manufacturer for subsea qualification testing, BRI must replace the standard commercial purchase order with a Conditional Prototype Evaluation Agreement. To ensure the research is not disqualified as "funded research" under I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the contract must explicitly stipulate that BRI retains all substantial intellectual property rights to the PHA-900X formula and polymerization technology without having to pay the customer for the right to use the research results, and that payment from the marine cable manufacturer is strictly contingent upon the pilot resin passing rigorous subsea dielectric and hydrostatic pressure acceptance testing, ensuring BRI bears the full financial risk of technical failure.

Third, all bio-monomers, custom metallocene catalysts, and solvents requisitioned for the quarantined PHA-900X pilot batches must be purchased under a dedicated R&D Pilot Material Requisition Code and expensed directly to an I.R.C. § 174 R&D expense account upon issuance, never entering commercial raw-material inventory or COGS. If any portion of Project Zeta involves pure process optimization on standard commercial batches after the PHA-900X formula is finalized and enters commercial production, BRI must strictly apply the Union Carbide rule to those subsequent runs by claiming only the incremental cost of the custom metallocene catalyst while excluding the baseline bio-monomers.
Step 3: Implementing the Shrinking-Back Rule and Systematic Experimentation Tracking

To prevent an all-or-nothing disqualification if one phase of the six-month campaign is challenged, BRI must embed the Shrinking-Back Rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and the scientific method directly into its engineering documentation. Rather than tracking all 18 batches under a single monolithic "Project Zeta" code, BRI must establish granular Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) sub-codes corresponding to discrete technical sub-components and uncertainties: WBS-Z1 for Metallocene Catalyst Stereoselectivity and Molecular Weight Distribution, WBS-Z2 for Cross-Linking Agent Dielectric Breakdown Resistance, and WBS-Z3 for Extrusion Melt-Fracture Rheology. If the IRS determines that WBS-Z3 involved routine equipment calibration lacking uncertainty under I.R.C. § 174, the disaggregated WBS cost tracking enables BRI to invoke Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and "shrink back" the claim to WBS-Z1 and WBS-Z2 without failing the 80 percent "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Simultaneously, for each of the 18 batches, BRI's polymer scientists must maintain a contemporaneous Design of Experiments (DoE) Matrix documenting the specific molecular weight or dielectric uncertainty targeted by that batch, the quantitative hypothesis being tested (such as altering the co-monomer feed ratio from 92:8 to 88:12 to suppress crystalline spherulite formation), the exact laboratory test results (including gel permeation chromatography, differential scanning calorimetry, and ASTM dielectric breakdown voltages), and the post-test analytical conclusion driving the formulation changes for the subsequent batch.
Step 4: Eliminating Unverified Consultant Estimates via Contemporaneous Verification Protocols

To avoid the evidentiary weaknesses seen in Union Carbide—where the Commissioner attacked Ms. Toivonen's failure to independently verify the MATRIC team's run durations and production quantities, the base-period figures were accepted only because UCC's concessions cured the methodological gaps, and the UCAT-J wage claim failed for lack of evidence of the time employees actually spent—BRI must abolish retrospective single-executive interviews. All polymer scientists, process engineers, and pilot-line technicians must record their hours bi-weekly against WBS-Z1, WBS-Z2, WBS-Z3, or Non-R&D Commercial Operations. At the close of each quarter, the Principal Polymer Scientist directly supervising Project Zeta must review the logged hours alongside the batch DoE logs and sign a contemporaneous I.R.C. § 6001 Technical Substantiation Certification verifying that every claimed hour and material requisition directly corresponded to an active experimental trial. Furthermore, any external tax advisor preparing the Form 6765 credit computation must independently audit the primary LIMS batch records, payroll registers, employee performance evaluations, and product cost records to confirm that non-qualifying commercial production activities and post-experimentation quality control runs are completely excised prior to filing.
Conclusion and Strategic Takeaways

The decisions of the United States Tax Court and the Second Circuit in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner establish an enduring doctrinal framework for industrial taxpayers seeking R&D tax credits under I.R.C. § 41. While the Plant Process Rule of I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) allows manufacturers to claim process improvement trials conducted on commercial equipment long after the underlying product has entered commercial production, Union Carbide strictly prohibits taxpayers from leveraging those process trials to sweep baseline raw materials, commercial inventory, and routine operator labor into the credit computation. By enforcing a rigorous demarcation between process improvements and pilot model products, documenting objective technological uncertainty prior to vendor chemical trials, executing complete post-test scientific data analyses, and maintaining contemporaneous sub-ledger cost and time tracking across both credit and base periods, United States taxpayers can fortify their research credit claims against IRS examination and judicial scrutiny.

metaDescription: Union Carbide v. Commissioner (T.C. 2009): raw materials a manufacturer would have bought anyway for commercial production are not research supplies.
